name: Eutropoflavin (7,8-DHF)
lead: 7,8-Dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), also called tropoflavin, is a naturally occurring flavone found in plants such as Godmania aesculifolia, Tridax procumbens and Primula vulgaris. It was reported in a 2010 PNAS paper as a small-molecule agonist of TrkB, the main receptor for brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).[1]

People who take it in supplement and recovery-oriented circles do so for BDNF-related effects: mood, focus, training recovery and body composition. The appearance-relevant research is in mice, where a 7,8-DHF treatment improved muscle mitochondrial function and reduced weight gain on a high-fat diet, which is the basis for interest in leaner body composition.[4][5] Muscle-derived BDNF has also been studied as a regulator of muscle mitochondrial quality.[4]

Sources differ on naming. Wikipedia uses the name eutropoflavin for the analogue 4'-dimethylamino-7,8-dihydroxyflavone and lists it among TrkB agonist analogues of 7,8-DHF,[1] while Grokipedia applies it to that analogue as a synthetic compound reported from Emory University work.[2] Supplement and recovery-oriented use often applies the name to 7,8-DHF itself. Published research on both is in cells and animals; no human trial was found.

angle.text: People take 7,8-DHF hoping to mimic BDNF signalling for mood, focus, recovery and body composition. The appearance-relevant work is in mice, where muscle BDNF and 7,8-DHF treatment were linked to mitochondrial function and weight gain on a high-fat diet.

paras: 7,8-DHF was described as a selective TrkB agonist with a dissociation constant of roughly 320 nM, and also as having antioxidant activity said to be independent of TrkB.[1] A 2017 line of work suggested it and other reported small-molecule TrkB agonists might not act as direct TrkB agonists.[1] In mice it is orally bioavailable (about 5%) with an elimination half-life under 30 minutes and crosses the blood-brain barrier.[1] The prodrug R13 has improved pharmacokinetics and is under development for Alzheimer's disease.[1]

In vitro, it is also reported as a weak aromatase inhibitor (Ki about 10 micromolar), an inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase (Ki about 35 micromolar) and of estrogen sulfotransferase (Ki about 1 to 3 micromolar), and anti-estrogenic only at very high concentrations; Wikipedia notes these effects were not confirmed in vivo, and that unlike many flavonoids it lacks inhibitory activity on 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase.[1] A 2016 review by the group that first reported it describes it as binding the extracellular domain of TrkB, triggering receptor dimerisation, and being orally bioactive and able to penetrate the blood-brain barrier.[3]

The primary report of 7,8-DHF as a TrkB agonist is the 2010 PNAS paper by Jang, Liu, Yepes and colleagues, with senior author Keqiang Ye of Emory University, titled as describing a selective TrkB agonist with potent neurotrophic activities.[1] Its authors framed the compound as a way around a core difficulty of BDNF as a drug, namely the lack of efficient means to deliver the protein into the body.[3] Prodrugs followed: Wikipedia names R7 and R13 (also called BrAD-R13 or Braegen-01), described as having greatly improved potency and pharmacokinetics and under development for Alzheimer's disease, and cites a 2018 PNAS paper on the prodrug's efficacy.[1]

In 2017 the compound's mechanism was questioned: evidence suggested that 7,8-DHF and several other reported small-molecule TrkB agonists might not be direct TrkB agonists and might act through other mechanisms.[1] A 2022 paper in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, titled as describing receptor-independent anti-ferroptotic activity of TrkB modulators, belongs to the same line of work on non-receptor effects.[8]

Reported animal-model results span depression, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's, Huntington's, ALS, traumatic brain injury, stroke, fragile X and Rett syndrome, plus improved memory in healthy rodents.[1][3] In mice it reduced dark-phase sleep and hypothalamic orexin A.[1] Grokipedia reports that the 4'-dimethylamino analogue promoted hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced immobility in forced-swim tests in mice.[2] In vitro it is a weak aromatase inhibitor, an effect not confirmed in vivo.[1]
A 2022 study reported that a TrkB agonist prodrug prevented bone loss in mice by acting on asparagine endopeptidase and osteoprotegerin.[6]

A 2015 review describes 7,8-DHF as a pro-neurotrophic candidate for neurodevelopmental disorders in which BDNF signalling is implicated, citing preclinical studies in which increasing BDNF signalling prevented or reversed abnormal neurodevelopmental events.[7] Reviewers have also discussed TrkB modulation in opioid tolerance, though those reviews concern TrkB as a target generally rather than 7,8-DHF specifically.[9]

A University of Hong Kong study in female mice found that obesity reduced BDNF in skeletal muscle and that mice lacking muscle BDNF gained more weight, burned less energy and developed worse insulin resistance on a high-fat diet, with damaged mitochondria accumulating in muscle. Treatment with 7,8-DHF eased mitochondrial dysfunction in obese mice, and the researchers suggested BDNF-signalling enhancers could be candidates for obesity treatment; the work was in mice.[4][5]

No human safety data were found. In mice the compound has low oral bioavailability of about 5 percent and a half-life under 30 minutes, which Wikipedia notes as a motivation for the prodrug approach.[1] The in vitro enzyme inhibition effects listed above have not been confirmed in vivo, and it has not been evaluated by regulators as a drug.[1]

Outside the laboratory, 7,8-DHF is sold as a dietary supplement in recovery- and cognition-oriented markets, where it is marketed on its BDNF association. No forum or media coverage focused on appearance use was identified, and the name eutropoflavin is applied inconsistently between the research analogue and 7,8-DHF products.
No studies found of 7,8-DHF in humans. Research is limited to cells and animals, with reviews summarising its potential for BDNF-implicated disorders.[3][7]

card.summary: A plant flavone reported to activate the BDNF receptor TrkB in animals; no human studies exist.
card.note: Animal-only evidence; whether it directly activates TrkB has been questioned.

quick.overview:
7,8-DHF is a flavone reported in 2010 to mimic BDNF signalling at the TrkB receptor. It is discussed for brain and mood effects and appears in recovery-oriented lists.

All published work found is in cells and animals, with a low oral bioavailability in mice. No human trial was found.
quick.mechanism: It is described as binding TrkB and triggering signalling such as AKT, though a 2017 line of work questioned direct agonism.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. Some in vitro effects, such as weak aromatase inhibition, have not been confirmed in living animals. It is not an approved drug.
